opus-5.5.text:
That's really the crux of it. If you take a high-resolution image and push it through a full encoder at every step, the cost explodes, and that's not acceptable for something you want to run on a phone or at interactive rates. So the first principle is: don't operate in pixel space any more than you absolutely have to.

What we do is work with a compact latent representation from the start. Rather than upsampling in pixel space and then encoding that big image, we encode the low-resolution input once into a latent with a much smaller spatial footprint, and do most of the heavy lifting there. Diffusion-style refinement or any iterative process happens on that compressed latent, so each step is cheap. Only at the end do we decode back to the full-resolution output.

The second piece is the encoder and decoder themselves. A standard VAE from a large generative model is quite heavy, so we've looked at lightweight, distilled versions, small enough to run fast but still faithful in the details that matter perceptually, like edges and textures. You can also be asymmetric: put more capacity in the decoder, where you need to hallucinate plausible high-frequency detail, and keep the encoder lean.

Third, we cut the number of steps. Iterative refinement with dozens of denoising steps is a non-starter for latency, so we use distillation to collapse the process into a handful of steps, sometimes a single one. The model learns to jump almost directly from the degraded latent to a clean one.

And finally, conditioning matters. The low-resolution image already contains most of the structure, so we don't start from pure noise. We start from a latent that's close to the answer, and the network only has to add the residual detail. That makes the problem easier and the computation smaller.

Put together, a compact latent, efficient encoders and decoders, very few steps, and strong conditioning on the input, you get the quality benefits of a generative approach without the slowness people usually associate with it.

fable-5.1.text:
Right, so the key thing is that you really don't want to run the heavy part of the network at the upsampled resolution. If you take, say, a 4K or 8K image and push it through a full encoder, you're paying a quadratic cost in attention or a very large cost in convolutions, and it just becomes impractical, especially on device.

So the way we think about it is, first, the latent space itself is already a compression. A VAE encoder typically brings you down by a factor of eight spatially, so a lot of the pixels are being folded into channels rather than being processed independently. That already gives you a big win. But even the encoder can be a bottleneck at high resolution, so we do a few things.

One is to make the encoder itself lightweight. A lot of the capacity in these models sits in the decoder and the diffusion backbone, so the encoder can be a much shallower network, and you can quantize it and run it on the NPU very efficiently.

The second is tiling. You split the image into overlapping patches, encode each patch independently, and stitch the latents back together. Because the encoder's receptive field is local, the result is nearly identical to encoding the whole image at once, but now the memory footprint is bounded and you can pipeline it.

The third, and this is the one I find most interesting, is that you often don't need to upsample first and then encode. If you're doing super-resolution, you encode the low-resolution image into latent space, and the upsampling happens in the latent domain, where it's much cheaper. Then the decoder produces the high-resolution output. So the expensive pixel-space upsampling is replaced by a latent-space operation on a tensor that's sixty-four times smaller.

And finally there's caching. In a lot of real applications the image doesn't change entirely between steps, so you can reuse latents from previous frames or previous edits and only re-encode the regions that changed. When you combine all of these, you can get the whole pipeline to run in a fraction of a second on a phone, which is where we want it to be.

r002.rationale: The response describes encoding overlapping patches, but does not say the patches match the original image’s dimensions.

astra-6.text:
The key is to avoid doing all the computation at the upsampled resolution. Upsampling gives you more pixels, but it doesn’t necessarily give you more information. So you can extract features from the lower-resolution image, map those into a compact latent representation, and do the expensive processing there. Then you reconstruct at the target resolution toward the end.

If you need to encode the upsampled image directly, you want to reduce the spatial dimensions early. But there’s a tradeoff: if you compress too aggressively, you lose the details you’re trying to recover. So the question is how to preserve useful image structure while keeping the latent representation small enough to process efficiently.

sol-6.1.text: The key is to avoid doing all the computation at the upsampled resolution. You first map the image into a compact latent representation, do the expensive processing there, and then decode it back into the image space. So you’re working with a much smaller spatial representation for most of the network. There’s still a cost to encoding and decoding, but you avoid carrying that high resolution through every layer. The tradeoff is making that latent representation compact enough to be efficient while preserving the details you need in the output.
